title: Digital Certificates and PKI
subtitle: X.509, certificate authorities, and trust chains

content.text: A digital certificate binds a public key to an identity, signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA). Your browser trusts hundreds of root CAs.

content.code:
# View a certificate
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text -noout

# Generate a self-signed certificate (for development)
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 \
  -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem \
  -days 365 -nodes \
  -subj "/CN=localhost"

# Get a free Let's Encrypt certificate
certbot --nginx -d example.com

content.definition: Root CA signs Intermediate CA signs your certificate. Browsers verify by walking up to a trusted root.

content.text: Use Let's Encrypt for free, automatically renewed certificates. Never pay for DV (domain validation) certificates.

questions.question: What does a Certificate Authority do?
options: Signs certificates to attest a public key belongs to a domain
questions.explanation: A CA verifies ownership of a domain and signs a certificate to establish trust.

faq.a: Hardcoding the expected certificate or public key in your app so it only trusts that specific cert, not any cert issued by any CA. Used in mobile apps to prevent MitM with rogue CA certs.
